claims.text: A supervised machine-learning framework can integrate experimental phonon dispersion and lifetime data with compositional and microstructural descriptors for high-entropy alloys.
The proposed model will predict low lattice thermal conductivity more accurately than conventional empirical or first-principles approaches.
Force-constant fluctuations caused by atomic disorder enhance phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys.
Mass fluctuations caused by atomic disorder enhance phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys.
Conventional empirical or first-principles methods typically miss the effects of mass and force-constant fluctuations on phonon scattering.
The intended material domain consists of single-phase, compositionally disordered FCC or BCC high-entropy alloys.
Phonon heat transport dominates in the stated moderate-to-high-temperature, thermal-insulation-relevant conditions.
Experimentally measured phonon linewidths and attenuation can serve as indicators of force-constant variability.
Phonon dispersion anomalies and linewidths can quantify mass fluctuations in high-entropy alloys.
Direct phonon measurements will allow the model to learn nonlinear correlations between local chemical disorder and phonon-scattering efficiency.
Short phonon lifetimes and reduced phonon group velocities are associated with low lattice thermal conductivity.
Enhanced disorder scattering reduces phonon mean free paths in high-entropy alloys.
High-entropy alloys with enhanced disorder scattering will have lower lattice thermal conductivity.
Conventional prediction methods have higher relative errors for complex disordered systems.
The model is expected to be applicable to homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The model's applicability is limited for multiphase or phase-segregated alloys.
Prediction improvement will depend on the quality, breadth, composition range, and disorder range represented in the training data.
Failure to achieve statistically lower lattice-thermal-conductivity prediction error than conventional models would falsify the hypothesis.
